claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 undergoes a complex, multistep crystallization sequence involving several crystalline phases during cooling.
The crystalline phases formed by the alloy are primary non-eutectic phases.
An isothermal hold immediately after rapid cooling will enhance amorphous retention and thermal stability.
The isothermal hold should be performed approximately 20–30 °C below the onset of primary crystallization.
Cooling at approximately 10^3 K/s or faster is required to initially suppress nucleation.
Slower cooling promotes formation of a more complex crystalline microstructure in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Rapid cooling reduces the number of crystalline phases, while very rapid melt spinning can produce an amorphous structure.
During the isothermal hold, the supercooled liquid undergoes structural relaxation.
Structural relaxation during the hold reduces diffusivity.
Structural relaxation during the hold lowers the nucleation driving force for crystallization.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses nucleation and subsequent growth of crystalline phases.
The hold modifies reheating kinetics and delays crystallization.
Samples receiving the hold will have a higher amorphous fraction and fewer primary crystalline phases than samples processed without the hold.
The intervention will shift or delay DSC crystallization peaks and reduce XRD-detectable crystallinity.
Without the hold, both rapid and slower cooling produce extensive primary crystallization.
Without the hold, the alloy has lower thermal stability.
The intervention is effective only when the hold remains within 20–30 °C below the primary crystallization onset.
The relevant reheating boundaries lie near the glass-transition and crystallization temperatures.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that the hold is applicable after rapid cooling and under slower-cooling processing, whereas the boundary states that cooling at about 10^3 K/s or faster is required for effectiveness.

The baseline says rapid cooling produces extensive primary crystallization, while the boundary and cited evidence indicate that rapid cooling reduces the phase count and very rapid melt spinning produces an amorphous structure.
